question: What is the main structural component found in the cell wall of fungi?
explanation: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, which gives them rigidity and separates them from bacteria that use peptidoglycan. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why do standard antibacterial medications fail to treat fungal infections?

options.A: Fungi live exclusively deep inside human tissue layers
options.B: Antibacterial drugs are always destroyed by stomach acid
options.C: Bacteria destroy the antibiotic before it can reach the fungi
options.D: Fungi have completely different cellular structures than bacteria

explanation: Antibacterial drugs target bacterial structures like peptidoglycan walls, which fungi do not possess. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h1)

question: What term describes fungi that only reproduce asexually in clinical laboratories?
explanation: Anamorphic fungi are those that lack a known sexual reproductive phase and reproduce strictly through asexual means. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h2)

question: How are major groups of fungi primarily distinguished from one another?

options.A: Their exact color when viewed without a microscope
options.B: The specific geographic region where they grow
options.C: The specific human organ they infect first
options.D: Their methods of sexual and asexual reproduction

explanation: Fungal groups are classified largely based on the specific structures they use to produce spores during reproduction. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which chemical preparation is commonly used to dissolve skin cells in a clinical sample so fungi can be seen?
explanation: A potassium hydroxide mount clears background human tissue debris in samples, making fungal structures much easier to see. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h3)

question: A laboratory report describes a cultured clinical sample as having a fuzzy, woolly appearance. What type of organism is most likely present?
explanation: Moulds produce fuzzy or woolly colonies because of their branching network of hyphae, whereas yeasts form smooth, creamy colonies. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the main method by which unicellular yeasts reproduce asexually?
explanation: Yeasts primarily reproduce by budding, where a new smaller cell grows out from the surface of the parent cell before separating. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h4)

question: What are pseudohyphae formed by yeast cells?

options.A: Hollow tubes created exclusively for absorbing water from soil
options.B: Chains of elongated yeast cells that remain attached after budding
options.C: Rigid mineral deposits found on the outside of fungal cell walls
options.D: Specialized reproductive organs that release swimming spores

explanation: Pseudohyphae occur when yeast buds fail to detach completely and grow longer, creating chains that resemble true fungal hyphae. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h4)

question: What name is given to hyphae that lack cross-walls and have a continuous cytoplasm with multiple nuclei?
explanation: Coenocytic hyphae lack internal cross-walls, allowing free movement of cytoplasm and cell parts throughout the filament. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h5)

question: How do conidia differ structurally from sporangiospores in moulds?

options.A: Conidia are borne externally on stalks, whereas sporangiospores are enclosed inside a sac
options.B: Conidia lack any outer protective wall, whereas sporangiospores have double walls
options.C: Conidia are strictly sexual spores, whereas sporangiospores are always asexual
options.D: Conidia are found only in underground roots, whereas sporangiospores float in air

explanation: Conidiospores develop openly on specialized hyphal branches, while sporangiospores develop within a protective sac called a sporangium. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h5)

question: At what temperature do dimorphic fungi typically grow in their mould form in the laboratory?
explanation: Dimorphic fungi grow as moulds at room temperature around 25 degrees Celsius and shift to yeast forms at body temperature around 37 degrees Celsius. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h6)

question: What triggers a dimorphic fungus to change from a mould to a yeast form?

options.A: Complete absence of oxygen in deep soil environments
options.B: High concentrations of carbon dioxide in water
options.C: Exposure to the higher temperature inside the human body

explanation: The shift from room temperature to human body temperature is the primary trigger for the fungus to change its form. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why must midwives exercise caution when considering systemic antifungal medications for pregnant women?

options.A: Antifungal drugs stop breast milk production permanently after birth
options.B: Certain oral antifungals can pose risks to the developing fetus
options.C: Systemic drugs cause immediate rupture of the amniotic membranes
options.D: Fungal cells in pregnant women are completely resistant to all medications

explanation: Some systemic antifungals can harm fetal development, making safety profiles a primary consideration during pregnancy. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h7)

question: A newborn infant develops white patches on the oral mucous membranes within the first week of life. What is the most likely source of this infection?

options.A: Acquisition from the mother's birth canal during vaginal delivery
options.B: Prolonged exposure to direct sunlight in the neonatal ward
options.C: An inherited genetic mutation passed down from the father
options.D: A side effect of routine Vitamin K injections given at birth

explanation: Neonatal oral thrush is frequently acquired as the baby passes through a birth canal colonized by Candida species. [learn more](BMP116_U3_T1#BMP116_U3_T1_h7)
